[[East Queensland Border languages|East Queensland Border]]? | fam3 = [[Kuric languages|Kuri]]? | dia1 = Yugambal | dia2 = Ngarbal | dia3 = [[Marbal]] | iso3 = yub | aiatsis = E11 | aiatsisname = Yugambal | aiatsis2 = E68 | aiatsisname2 = Ngarbal | aiatsisname3 = Marbal | aiatsis3 = E91 | glotto = yuga1244 | glottorefname = Yugambal }} '''Yugambal''' (Yugumbal, Jukambal), or '''Yugumbil''' (Jukambil), is an [[Australian Aboriginal languages|Australian Aboriginal language]] of northern [[New South Wales]]. The name is derived from the word ''juka'', meaning 'no'.{{sfn|Tindale|1974}} == Classification == Yugambal may have been a [[Kuric language]]. However, it has been confused with the Bundjalung dialect of [[Yugambeh language|Yugambeh]] in the literature, muddling accounts of its classification. Yugumbil is, however, considered a dialect of [[Yugambeh–Bundjalung languages|Bandjalang]]. It has also been grouped with [[Yagara language|Yagara]], [[Janday language|Janday]], [[Guyambal language|Guyambal]] and [[Bigambal language|Bigambal]].{{Cite book |last1=Wafer |first1=James William |url=https://www.worldcat.org/title/271859989 |title=A handbook of Aboriginal languages of New South Wales and the Australian Capital Territory |last2=Lissarrague |first2=Amanda |date=2008 |publisher=Muurrbay Aboriginal Language & Culture Co-operative |isbn=978-0-9775351-8-7 |location=Nambucca Heads, N.S.W |oclc=271859989}} == History == As late as 1855, people speaking the Jukambal language were encountered living on the [[Macintyre River]].{{sfn|Tindale|1974}} == Geographical distribution == Macpherson (1905)Macpherson, J. (1905). Ngarrabul and other Aboriginal Tribes. Proceedings of the Linnean Society of New South Wales, 29, 677 - 684 describes the Yugambal language as prevailing from Boggy Camp and Inverell, almost to Bingara on the west, Bundarra on the south, and Tingha on the south-east. He further notes that the [[Ngarabal|Ngarrabul]], Marbul, and Yugambal people understood each other, as did [[Ngarabal|Ngarrabul]], Kwiambal and Yugambal, so they are assumed to have spoken dialects of a single language. Dixon also gives Ngarrabul or Ngarrbal as a dialect of the Yugambal language.Dixon, RMW (1976). Grammatical Categories in Australian Languages. Australian Institute of Aboriginal Studies: CanberraDixon, RMW. (2004). Australian Languages, Their Nature and Development, Volume 1. Cambridge University Press, Cambridge UK. == Status == The status of the language is uncertain. Some known language speakers, including Sira Draper, Hughie Green and Archie Green, were alive in the mid-to-late 20th century. However, it is unknown whether there are any other speakers.{{Cite journal |last=Austin |first=Peter K. |title=A Reference Grammar of Gamilaraay, northern New South Wales |url=https://www.academia.edu/2457676}}Howell, R. 1983, The History and Culture of the Aboriginal People of the Ashford District, D West Government Printers: NSW. == Documentation == There is little description of the language.
